lessons.title: Cardiac Cycle**, Left Ventricular Pressure-Volume Changes* & Heart Sounds*

slides.h: 1. Definition, Duration & Phases of Cardiac Cycle
slides.p: The cardiac cycle is the sequence of coordinated mechanical and electrical events occurring in the heart during one heartbeat. At a resting heart rate of 75 beats/min, one cycle lasts 0.8 seconds (Atrial systole = 0.1 s, Atrial diastole = 0.7 s; Ventricular systole = 0.3 s, Ventricular diastole = 0.5 s):
bullets: 1. Atrial Systole (0.1 s): Atria contract, adding the final ~20–30% ('atrial kick') to ventricular filling; AV valves open, semilunar valves closed; produces a-wave in JVP and 4th heart sound (S4).
2. Isovolumetric Ventricular Contraction (0.05 s): Begins with closure of AV valves (S1); all 4 valves closed; ventricular pressure rises steeply while volume remains constant at EDV (~120–130 mL).
3. Ventricular Ejection (0.25 s): Opens when LV pressure >80 mmHg (RV >8 mmHg); Rapid ejection (0.1 s) ejects ~2/3 of stroke volume (peak LV pressure = 120 mmHg); Reduced ejection (0.15 s).
4. Protodiastole (0.04 s) & Isovolumetric Relaxation (0.08 s): Semilunar valves snap shut (S2); all 4 valves closed; LV pressure falls precipitously while volume stays constant at ESV (~50 mL).
5. Ventricular Filling Phases (0.38 s): AV valves open → First rapid filling (0.11 s) (produces S3) → Diastasis / Slow filling (0.19 s) → followed by next atrial systole.
slides.remember: At 75 bpm = 0.8 s! EDV = 120 mL, ESV = 50 mL, Stroke Volume = 70 mL (Ejection Fraction ~58–60%)!
slides.q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does left ventricular pressure rise steeply while ventricular volume remains constant?
slides.why: During isovolumetric contraction (0.05 s), both AV and semilunar valves are closed, so LV pressure surges from ~5 mmHg to >80 mmHg with no change in blood volume.

slides.h: 2. Left Ventricular Pressure-Volume Loop* & Four Heart Sounds*
slides.p: On the LV Pressure-Volume (Wiggers / P-V) Loop, four corners mark valve events, and four heart sounds correspond to specific mechanical vibrations:
bullets: P-V Loop Corners: A (Mitral valve closes) → AB = Isovolumetric contraction → B (Aortic valve opens at ~80 mmHg) → BC = Ejection (peaks at 120 mmHg) → C (Aortic valve closes) → CD = Isovolumetric relaxation → D (Mitral valve opens) → DA = Diastolic filling. Area inside loop = External Stroke Work.
1st Heart Sound (S1 — 'Lubb'): Closure of AV (mitral & tricuspid) valves at onset of ventricular systole; low-pitched, prolonged (0.15 s), 25–45 Hz.
2nd Heart Sound (S2 — 'Dupp'): Closure of semilunar (aortic & pulmonary) valves at onset of diastole; high-pitched, sharp (0.12 s), 50 Hz; physiological splitting on inspiration (A2 before P2).
3rd Heart Sound (S3): Rapid rush of blood hitting ventricular walls during first rapid filling phase (normal in children/athletes; gallop rhythm in heart failure).
4th Heart Sound (S4): Atrial contraction pushing blood into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle (always pathological in adults, e.g., LV hypertrophy).
slides.remember: S1 = AV close ('Lubb'). S2 = Semilunar close ('Dupp'). S3 = Rapid filling rush. S4 = Atrial kick into stiff ventricle!
slides.q: Which phase of the cardiac cycle is directly responsible for generating the third heart sound (S3)?
slides.why: S3 is produced by oscillations of blood and ventricular walls during the rapid inflow of blood in the first rapid filling phase of ventricular diastole.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition & normal duration (0.8 s at 75 bpm) → Table/timeline of atrial & ventricular phases (duration, valve status, pressure & volume changes) → Left ventricular Pressure-Volume loop diagram → Heart sounds (S1, S2, S3, S4) + Wiggers diagram.

lessons.title: Properties of Cardiac Muscle*, SA Node Autorhythmicity & Non-Tetanizability

slides.h: 1. Five Cardinal Properties & Ionic Basis of SA Node Pacemaker Potential
slides.p: Cardiac muscle exhibits five key physiological properties: Excitability, Rhythmicity (Autorhythmicity), Conductivity, Contractility, and All-or-None Law / Staircase phenomenon:
bullets: SA Node Pacemaker Potential (Prepotential): SA node has an unstable resting potential (~−55 to −60 mV) that drifts slowly upward to firing threshold (−40 mV) via three ion currents: 1. Funny Na⁺ channels (If) open on hyperpolarization (slow inward Na⁺ leak), 2. Decay of K⁺ efflux, and 3. Transient T-type Ca²⁺ channels opening just before threshold.
Action Potential Upstroke & Repolarization in SA Node: Depolarization is caused by L-type Ca²⁺ influx (NOT fast Na⁺ channels!); repolarization is caused by K⁺ efflux.
Conduction Velocities: Purkinje fibers = fastest (~4 m/s); AV node = slowest (~0.05 m/s, 0.1 s delay allowing complete atrial emptying before ventricular contraction).
slides.remember: SA node prepotential = Funny Na⁺ (If) + ↓K⁺ efflux + T-type Ca²⁺! Upstroke = L-type Ca²⁺! AV node = Slowest (0.1 s delay)!
slides.q: Which ion channel initiates the slow diastolic depolarization (prepotential) in the SA node?
opts: Funny Na⁺ channels (If) activated by hyperpolarization
slides.why: Hyperpolarization at the end of repolarization opens hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 'funny' (If) Na⁺ channels, initiating the pacemaker prepotential.

slides.h: 2. Why Cardiac Muscle Cannot Be Tetanized
slides.p: A classic short-note and viva question asks why skeletal muscle can undergo sustained tetanic contraction whereas cardiac muscle cannot:
bullets: Long Plateau Phase (Phase 2): Ventricular action potential lasts 250–300 ms due to slow L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux.

Prolonged Absolute Refractory Period (ARP): Because the ARP (~200–250 ms) spans almost the entire duration of mechanical contraction and early relaxation, a second stimulus cannot re-excite the myocardium until it has already relaxed.
Physiological Significance: Prevents sustained spasm (tetanus) of the heart, guaranteeing adequate diastolic filling time between beats.
slides.remember: Long Plateau (Ca²⁺ influx) → Long Absolute Refractory Period lasting throughout contraction → Heart CANNOT be tetanized!
slides.q: Why is it impossible to tetanize cardiac muscle even with high-frequency electrical stimulation?
opts: Its prolonged absolute refractory period lasts almost throughout the entire contraction phase
slides.why: The plateau phase (L-type Ca²⁺ influx) prolongs the absolute refractory period across nearly the entire twitch contraction, preventing summation or tetanus.

lessons.title: ECG (Limb Leads, Lead II Trace* & Heart Block)

slides.h: 1. Bipolar & Unipolar Limb Leads (Einthoven's Triangle)
slides.p: An electrocardiogram (ECG) records the algebraic sum of cardiac action potentials from the body surface using 12 standard leads (6 limb + 6 chest):
bullets: Bipolar Limb Leads (Einthoven): Lead I: Left Arm (+) vs Right Arm (−); Lead II: Left Leg (+) vs Right Arm (−) (largest upright R wave, parallel to mean cardiac vector!); Lead III: Left Leg (+) vs Left Arm (−). Einthoven's Law: Lead II = Lead I + Lead III.
Augmented Unipolar Limb Leads: aVR (+ on Right Arm), aVL (+ on Left Arm), aVF (+ on Left Foot) — indifferent electrode connects the other two limbs through 5000-ohm resistors.
slides.remember: Einthoven's Law: Lead II = Lead I + Lead III! Lead II has Left Leg (+) and Right Arm (−)!
slides.q: According to Einthoven's law, which mathematical relationship holds true for the standard bipolar limb leads?
opts: Lead I = Lead II + Lead III
Lead II = Lead I + Lead III
Lead III = Lead I + Lead II
Lead I + Lead II + Lead III = 1
slides.why: Einthoven's law states that the potential in Lead II equals the sum of potentials in Lead I and Lead III (II = I + III).

slides.h: 2. Normal ECG Trace in Lead II* (Waves, Intervals & Segments)
slides.p: Draw and label every wave, interval, and segment of a normal Lead II ECG:
bullets: P Wave: Atrial depolarization (0.08–0.10 s, <2.5 mm).
PR Interval (0.12–0.20 s / 3–5 small squares): Onset of P to onset of QRS; represents atrial depolarization + AV nodal delay.
QRS Complex (0.08–0.10 s): Ventricular depolarization (masks atrial repolarization).
ST Segment (Isoelectric): Ventricular plateau phase (elevation = acute MI; depression = ischemia).
T Wave: Ventricular repolarization (upright in Lead II because epicardium repolarizes before endocardium).
QT Interval (~0.35–0.43 s): Total ventricular depolarization + repolarization.
slides.remember: PR interval = 0.12–0.20 s (AV nodal delay)! QRS = <0.10 s! ST elevation = Acute MI!
slides.q: What is the normal duration of the PR interval in a standard Lead II ECG?
slides.why: A normal PR interval lasts 0.12 to 0.20 seconds (3 to 5 small squares at 25 mm/s) and reflects AV nodal conduction delay.

slides.h: 3. Heart Block — Classification & AV Nodal Block
slides.p: Heart block is impaired or interrupted impulse conduction anywhere from the SA node to the Purkinje system:
bullets: Types: Sinoatrial (SA) block, Atrioventricular (AV) nodal block, and Bundle branch block (RBBB / LBBB).
1st-Degree AV Block: Prolonged PR interval (>0.20 s), every P wave followed by QRS.
2nd-Degree AV Block: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) — progressive PR lengthening until a QRS drops; Mobitz Type II — fixed PR with sudden dropped QRS beats (e.g., 2:1 or 3:1 block).

3rd-Degree (Complete) AV Block: Complete AV dissociation — atria beat at SA rate (~75/min), ventricles beat independently via slow idioventricular rhythm (~30–40/min); sudden cerebral hypoxia causes Stokes-Adams syncopal attacks.
slides.remember: 1st° = PR >0.20 s. 2nd° Wenckebach = PR gets longer, longer, drops! 3rd° Complete = P and QRS completely divorced + Stokes-Adams attacks!
slides.q: Progressive prolongation of the PR interval followed by a dropped QRS complex is characteristic of:
opts: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) second-degree AV block
slides.why: Wenckebach (Mobitz Type I) AV nodal block shows progressive lengthening of the PR interval on successive beats until one atrial impulse fails to conduct.

lessons.title: Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume, Venous Return & Fick Principle

slides.h: 1. Definitions, Normal Values & Fick Principle
slides.p: Memorize the exact definitions, formulas, and normal resting adult values:
bullets: Stroke Volume (SV): Volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per beat = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = 70 mL/beat.
Cardiac Output (CO): Volume pumped by each ventricle per minute = SV × HR = 70 mL × 72/min ≈ 5 L/min.
Cardiac Index (CI): CO per square meter of body surface area (1.7 m²) = 5 / 1.7 ≈ 3.0–3.2 L/min/m²; Stroke Volume Index = SV / BSA ≈ 41 mL/beat/m².

Fick Principle: Blood flow to an organ equals amount of substance taken up (or released) per minute divided by its arteriovenous concentration difference: CO = O₂ consumption (250 mL/min) / [Arterial O₂ (200 mL/L) − Mixed Venous O₂ (150 mL/L)] = 250 / 50 = 5 L/min.
slides.remember: CO = SV × HR (70 × 72 ≈ 5 L/min)! Cardiac Index ≈ 3.2 L/min/m²! Fick = O₂ uptake (250) / A-V O₂ diff (50) = 5 L/min!
slides.q: Using the Fick principle, if whole-body O₂ consumption is 250 mL/min, arterial O₂ content is 200 mL/L, and mixed venous O₂ content is 150 mL/L, what is the cardiac output?

slides.h: 2. Factors Affecting Stroke Volume, Venous Return & Cardiac Output
slides.p: Cardiac output is regulated by Heart Rate and Stroke Volume (Preload, Contractility, Afterload):
bullets: 1. Preload (Venous Return — Frank-Starling Law): Force of contraction is directly proportional to initial length of myocardial fibers (EDV) within physiological limits.

2. Factors Promoting Venous Return (6): Skeletal muscle pump (calf veins + valves), Respiratory pump (negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration), Cardiac suction (ventricular systole pulling AV ring down), Venomotor tone (sympathetic venoconstriction), Blood volume, and Gravity/Posture.
3. Myocardial Contractility (Inotropy): Increased by sympathetic stimulation (β₁), circulating catecholamines, Ca²⁺, digitalis; decreased by hypoxia, acidosis, β-blockers.
4. Afterload: Aortic diastolic pressure / total peripheral resistance opposing LV ejection (Anrep effect).
slides.remember: SV determinants = Preload (Frank-Starling / Venous return) + Contractility (Inotropy) + Afterload (TPR)!
slides.q: According to the Frank-Starling law of the heart, within physiological limits, the force of ventricular contraction is directly proportional to:
slides.why: Increased venous return stretches ventricular muscle fibers (higher EDV), optimizing actin-myosin overlap and increasing stroke volume.

lessons.title: Blood Pressure Regulation (Baroreceptor Reflex, CNS Ischemic Response, RAAS & JGA)

slides.h: 1. Short-Term Neural Control: Baroreceptor Reflex & CNS Ischemic Response
slides.p: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) = Diastolic BP + 1/3 Pulse Pressure (~93 mmHg) = CO × Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR). Rapid second-to-second regulation is neural:
bullets: Baroreceptor (Sinoaortic) Reflex (Active at MAP 60–180 mmHg): High-pressure stretch receptors in Carotid Sinus (via Hering's nerve → CN IX) and Aortic Arch (via Aortic depressor nerve → CN X) project to Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS). When BP rises → NTS stimulates Nucleus Ambiguus (Vagus → ↓HR) and inhibits RVLM vasomotor center (↓Sympathetic → vasodilation & ↓TPR) → restores BP!
Chemoreceptor Reflex (MAP <80 mmHg): Carotid & aortic bodies respond to hypoxia/hypercapnia/H⁺ by stimulating RVLM to raise BP.

CNS Ischemic Response ('Last-Ditch Stand' — MAP <60 mmHg, maximal at 15–20 mmHg): Severe brainstem ischemia accumulates CO₂/lactic acid in vasomotor center → massive sympathetic discharge raising MAP up to 250 mmHg (Cushing reflex when raised ICP compresses medullary vessels: hypertension + reflex bradycardia!).
slides.remember: Baroreceptor = Buffer nerves (CN IX from carotid sinus, CN X from aortic arch) → NTS! CNS Ischemic Response = Last-ditch stand at MAP <60 mmHg!
slides.q: Which cranial nerves carry afferent impulses from the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)?
slides.why: Carotid sinus baroreceptors signal via Hering's branch of CN IX, and aortic arch baroreceptors signal via the aortic branch of CN X to the medullary NTS.

slides.h: 2. Long-Term Renal-Body Fluid Control: JGA & Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
slides.p: Long-term BP is governed by kidney fluid volume and the Juxtaglomerular Apparatus (JGA):
bullets: Three Stimuli for Renin Release from JG Cells: 1. ↓Renal perfusion pressure (afferent arteriolar baroreceptors), 2. ↓NaCl delivery to Macula Densa, and 3. ↑Sympathetic β₁ stimulation.
RAAS Cascade: Renin converts Angiotensinogen (liver) → Angiotensin I → converted in pulmonary capillaries by ACE → Angiotensin II.

Actions of Angiotensin II: Potent arteriolar vasoconstrictor (↑TPR), stimulates Aldosterone from zona glomerulosa (↑Na⁺ & water reabsorption in principal cells of collecting duct), stimulates ADH & thirst, and enhances proximal Na⁺ reabsorption.
slides.remember: Renin (JGA) → Angiotensin I → ACE → Angiotensin II (Vasoconstriction + Aldosterone + ADH + Thirst) → Long-term BP rise!
slides.q: Which enzyme converts inactive Angiotensin I into active Angiotensin II primarily in the pulmonary capillary endothelium?
slides.why: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), abundant on pulmonary vascular endothelium, cleaves Angiotensin I to form the potent vasoconstrictor Angiotensin II.

lessons.title: Circulatory Shock** (Classification, Stages & Physiological Management)

slides.h: 1. Definition, Classification & Three Stages of Shock
slides.p: Circulatory shock is a life-threatening clinical syndrome of generalized inadequate tissue perfusion leading to cellular hypoxia and organ dysfunction:
bullets: Classification (4 Types): 1. Hypovolemic shock (hemorrhage, severe burns, vomiting/diarrhea), 2. Cardiogenic shock (massive MI, arrhythmias, tamponade), 3. Distributive / Vasogenic shock (Septic/endotoxic shock, Anaphylactic shock [IgE histamine], Neurogenic shock [loss of sympathetic tone]), and 4. Obstructive shock (massive pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax).

Stage 1 — Non-Progressive (Compensated) Stage (<10–15% blood loss): Negative-feedback reflexes restore CO & BP: Baroreceptor reflex (tachycardia, arteriolar & venous constriction), RAAS & ADH (fluid conservation), and Capillary fluid shift (absorption of interstitial fluid into plasma).

Stage 2 — Progressive Stage: Positive-feedback vicious cycles take over — myocardial ischemia depresses CO, vasomotor failure, capillary endothelial hypoxia increases permeability (fluid leaks out), sludging/DIC, and metabolic lactic acidosis.
Stage 3 — Irreversible Stage: Severe cellular ATP depletion, lysosomal enzyme release, and multiorgan failure refractory even to full blood transfusion.
slides.remember: 3 Stages: Compensated (Negative feedback wins) → Progressive (Positive feedback vicious cycles) → Irreversible (ATP depletion refractory to transfusion)!
slides.q: Which physiological mechanism in the compensated stage of hemorrhagic shock shifts interstitial fluid into the intravascular capillary compartment?
opts: Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure due to arteriolar vasoconstriction
Increased plasma albumin synthesis within 5 minutes
slides.why: Sympathetic arteriolar vasoconstriction lowers capillary hydrostatic pressure below plasma colloid osmotic pressure, drawing interstitial fluid into capillaries ('autotransfusion').

slides.h: 2. Physiological Principles of Management of Hemorrhagic Shock
slides.p: Every treatment step directly targets the underlying physiological derangement:
bullets: 1. Posture (Trendelenburg / Leg Elevation): Foot-end elevation (~15–20°) promotes venous return by gravity without impairing diaphragmatic breathing.

2. Volume Replacement (Restoring Preload): Whole blood / packed RBCs for hemorrhagic shock; crystalloids (normal saline / Ringer's lactate) or plasma expanders (dextran/albumin) to restore EDV and CO.
3. Oxygenation & Acidosis Correction: 100% O₂ inhalation + sodium bicarbonate if severe lactic acidosis depresses myocardial contractility.
4. Judicious Vasopressors / Inotropes & Steroids: Dopamine/norepinephrine (only after volume replacement) and glucocorticoids (stabilize lysosomal & capillary membranes in septic/anaphylactic shock).
slides.remember: Management pillars = Leg elevation + Restore blood/fluid volume + O₂ + Correct acidosis!
slides.q: Why should potent vasoconstrictors (like norepinephrine) NOT be given alone before fluid resuscitation in hypovolemic shock?
opts: They worsen tissue ischemia by constricting arterioles when intravascular volume is still depleted
slides.why: In hypovolemic shock, sympathetic vasoconstriction is already maximal; adding vasopressors without restoring blood volume further reduces tissue perfusion.

lessons.title: Coronary Circulation & Angina Pectoris

slides.h: 1. Physiological Anatomy & Five Special Features of Coronary Circulation
slides.p: At rest, the heart receives ~250 mL/min (~5% of cardiac output) via the right and left coronary arteries and exhibits five hallmark physiological features:
bullets: 1. Phasic Flow — Predominantly Diastolic in Left Ventricle: During LV systole, intense intramyocardial pressure (~120+ mmHg) compresses subendocardial vessels, briefly arresting or reversing LV coronary flow; ~80% of LV coronary blood flow occurs during diastole! (Tachycardia shortens diastole and compromises LV perfusion!).

2. High Basal O₂ Extraction (~70–80%): Coronary venous blood is already heavily desaturated (O₂ content ~5 mL/100 mL), so increased myocardial O₂ demand during exercise MUST be met by coronary vasodilation (increasing flow 4–5 fold).
3. Metabolic Autoregulation (Primary Controller): Local vasodilator metabolites—especially Adenosine, K⁺, H⁺, CO₂, and hypoxia—directly dilate coronary arterioles.
4. Functional End-Arteries: Sudden coronary occlusion causes myocardial infarction (subendocardial region is most vulnerable!).
5. Sympathetic Paradox: Direct α-receptors constrict, while β₂-receptors & metabolic vasodilators produced by β₁-mediated ↑HR/contractility cause net coronary vasodilation.
slides.remember: LV gets 80% of its blood during DIASTOLE! Adenosine = #1 metabolic coronary vasodilator! High O₂ extraction (75%)!
slides.q: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does the left ventricular myocardium receive the vast majority (~80%) of its coronary blood flow?
slides.why: Strong systolic contraction of the thick left ventricle compresses intramural vessels; therefore, LV coronary perfusion occurs predominantly during diastole.

slides.h: 2. Angina Pectoris & Physiological Basis of Nitrate Therapy
slides.p: Angina pectoris is paroxysmal retrosternal squeezing chest pain caused by transient myocardial ischemia (O₂ demand > O₂ supply):
bullets: Mechanism of Pain & Radiation: Anaerobic glycolysis accumulates adenosine, bradykinin, lactate, and Substance P, stimulating cardiac sympathetic afferents (T1–T4) → referred pain to precordium and inner border of left arm (dermatomal rule).

Physiological Action of Sublingual Nitroglycerin (GTN): Releases Nitric Oxide (NO) → primarily causes venodilation (reduces venous return/preload and ventricular wall tension = ↓myocardial O₂ demand) + dilates epicardial collateral coronary arteries.
slides.remember: Nitroglycerin relieves angina primarily by VENODILATION (reducing Preload & LV wall tension), thereby lowering myocardial O₂ demand!
slides.q: What is the primary physiological mechanism by which sublingual nitroglycerin relieves an acute attack of angina pectoris?
opts: Venodilation reducing venous return (preload) and myocardial O₂ demand
slides.why: Nitrates predominantly dilate systemic capacitance veins, reducing venous return (preload), ventricular end-diastolic volume, and myocardial oxygen consumption.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Physiologic anatomy & normal flow (250 mL/min) → Five special features (phasic diastolic flow diagram, high O₂ extraction, metabolic autoregulation via adenosine, functional end-arteries) → Angina pectoris (pathophysiology, referred pain T1–T4, nitrate mechanism).

lessons.title: Regulation of Heart Rate & Cardiovascular Effects of Muscular Exercise

slides.h: 1. Regulation of Heart Rate & Bainbridge Reflex
slides.p: Normal resting heart rate is 60–100 bpm (average 72 bpm), governed by dominant resting vagal (parasympathetic) tone:
bullets: Vagal Tone (Right Vagus → SA Node): Acetylcholine opens M₂ K⁺ channels (hyperpolarizes SA node) → ↓HR. Cutting both vagi raises HR to ~100–110 bpm (intrinsic SA rate).
Sympathetic Drive (T1–T4 → β₁ receptors): Increases If & Ca²⁺ currents → steepens prepotential slope → ↑HR.

Reflexes: Marey's Law (HR is inversely proportional to BP via baroreceptors); Bainbridge Reflex (rapid IV infusion stretches right atrial stretch receptors → vagal afferents inhibit cardiac vagal center → ↑HR); Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia (HR increases on inspiration, decreases on expiration).
slides.remember: Marey's Law = ↑BP → ↓HR! Bainbridge Reflex = ↑Right atrial stretch → ↑HR! Inspiration = ↑HR!
slides.q: Which reflex explains the increase in heart rate following rapid intravenous saline infusion that stretches the right atrium?
slides.why: Stretch of right atrial volume receptors by increased venous return triggers the Bainbridge reflex, increasing heart rate.

slides.h: 2. Why Heart Rate Increases & How BP Changes in Isotonic Exercise
slides.p: Muscular exercise triggers immediate, integrated cardiovascular adjustments:
bullets: 4 Mechanisms Increasing HR in Exercise: 1. Central command (cortical impulses to medullary cardiovascular centers even before exercise starts!), 2. Withdrawal of vagal tone (responsible for initial rapid rise up to ~100 bpm) followed by sympathetic stimulation, 3. Muscle mechanoreceptors & metaboreceptors (ergoreceptors), and 4. Bainbridge reflex + ↑body temperature.

Effect of Isotonic (Dynamic) Exercise on BP: Systolic BP rises markedly (up to 160–180 mmHg due to ↑CO up to 20–25 L/min); Diastolic BP remains unchanged or falls slightly (due to massive metabolic vasodilation in active skeletal muscles lowering TPR!); hence Pulse Pressure widens!
slides.remember: Isotonic exercise: Systolic BP ↑↑, Diastolic BP ↔ or ↓ (muscle vasodilation lowers TPR), Pulse Pressure widens!
slides.q: During moderate isotonic (dynamic) exercise such as running, what happens to systolic and diastolic blood pressure?
opts: Both systolic and diastolic BP fall sharply
Systolic BP increases markedly while diastolic BP stays unchanged or falls slightly
Diastolic BP rises markedly while systolic BP falls
Neither systolic nor diastolic BP changes
slides.why: In isotonic exercise, increased cardiac output raises systolic BP, while metabolic vasodilation in active skeletal muscle reduces total peripheral resistance, keeping diastolic BP unchanged or slightly lower.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Definition of HR & vagal tone → Factors regulating HR (neural, medullary centers, baroreceptor/Marey's, Bainbridge, chemical/hormonal) → Mechanisms of exercise tachycardia → Effect of isotonic vs isometric exercise on SBP, DBP, MAP & Pulse Pressure.

lessons.title: Deglutition (Pharyngeal Phase**) & Achalasia Cardia

slides.h: 1. Three Phases of Deglutition & Pharyngeal Phase** Events
slides.p: Deglutition (swallowing) is a coordinated reflex transporting food from the mouth to the stomach in three phases:
bullets: 1. Oral (Buccal) Phase (Voluntary): Tongue presses upward and backward against hard palate, pushing bolus into oropharynx.

2. Pharyngeal Phase** (Involuntary Reflex — <1–2 s): Bolus stimulates tactile receptors on tonsillar pillars → afferents via CN V, IX, X to medullary swallowing center → efferents via CN V, IX, X, XII trigger 4 simultaneous protective closures: (a) Soft palate elevates (closes nasopharynx), (b) Vocal cords adduct + epiglottis swings backward + larynx elevates (closes airway), (c) Deglutition apnea (brief inhibition of respiration for 1–2 s), and (d) Upper esophageal sphincter (UES) relaxes while pharyngeal constrictors propel bolus into esophagus.

3. Esophageal Phase (Involuntary): Primary peristalsis (continuation of pharyngeal wave, 8–10 s) and Secondary peristalsis (triggered by local esophageal distension) + receptive relaxation of Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES) via VIP & Nitric Oxide.
slides.remember: Pharyngeal Phase** closes ALL 3 wrong exits (nose, mouth, larynx) + causes Deglutition Apnea + relaxes UES!
slides.q: Which two neurotransmitters mediate receptive relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) during swallowing?
opts: Vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) and Nitric Oxide (NO)
slides.why: Inhibitory myenteric neurons release VIP and nitric oxide (NO) to relax the smooth muscle of the lower esophageal sphincter.

slides.h: 2. Importance of Deglutition Reflex & Achalasia Cardia
slides.p: Complete your answer with the protective significance of the reflex and its classic motility disorder:
bullets: Importance of Deglutition Reflex: Prevents nasal regurgitation and life-threatening aspiration pneumonia during swallowing (loss in bulbar palsy or deep coma risks aspiration).

Achalasia Cardia: Neuromuscular disorder caused by degeneration/absence of inhibitory VIP/NO neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus of the lower esophagus → LES fails to relax during swallowing + aperistalsis of esophageal body → progressive dysphagia (for both solids and liquids), regurgitation, and classic 'bird-beak' tapering on barium swallow.
slides.remember: Achalasia Cardia = Loss of inhibitory VIP/NO myenteric neurons → LES stays tightly closed ('bird-beak' on barium swallow)!
slides.q: Achalasia cardia is primarily caused by degeneration of inhibitory neurons releasing which mediators in the esophageal myenteric plexus?
slides.why: Loss of VIP- and nitric oxide-producing inhibitory myenteric ganglion cells prevents lower esophageal sphincter relaxation in achalasia cardia.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Definition → Three phases → Detailed Pharyngeal Phase** (afferents, swallowing center, 4 protective airway/nasal closures, deglutition apnea) → Esophageal peristalsis & LES → Importance of reflex → Achalasia cardia (pathophysiology, features, barium 'bird-beak', treatment).

lessons.title: Gastric Juice, HCl Secretion*** & Peptic Ulcer***

slides.h: 1. Gastric Glands & Mechanism of HCl Secretion*** by Parietal Cells
slides.p: The stomach secretes 1.5–2.5 L/day of gastric juice (pH 1.0–2.0) from tubular gastric glands containing Mucous neck cells (mucus/HCO₃⁻), Chief/Peptic cells (pepsinogen & gastric lipase), Parietal/Oxyntic cells (HCl & Castle's Intrinsic Factor), and G-cells / ECL cells:
bullets: Step-by-Step HCl Secretion in Parietal Cells: 1. Inside parietal cell, Carbonic Anhydrase hydrates CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. 2. Apical H⁺–K⁺ ATPase (Proton Pump) actively pumps H⁺ into canaliculus in exchange for K⁺. 3. Basolateral Cl⁻–HCO₃⁻ exchanger exports HCO₃⁻ into venous blood (causing postprandial 'alkaline tide') and imports Cl⁻, which exits apically via cAMP-gated Cl⁻ channels to form HCl!
Three Receptors Stimulating Parietal Cell: 1. Acetylcholine (M₃ — vagus) via IP₃/Ca²⁺, 2. Gastrin (CCK-B) via IP₃/Ca²⁺, and 3. Histamine from ECL cells (H₂) via cAMP (potentiates ACh & Gastrin!).
slides.remember: Apical Proton Pump = H⁺–K⁺ ATPase! Basolateral HCO₃⁻ exit = Postprandial Alkaline Tide! 3 parietal stimulators = ACh (M₃), Gastrin (CCK-B), Histamine (H₂)!
slides.q: Which apical transport protein directly secretes H⁺ ions into the gastric lumen from parietal cells?
slides.why: The apical H⁺–K⁺ ATPase actively pumps H⁺ into the secretory canaliculus in exchange for K⁺, generating gastric pH ~1.

slides.h: 2. Three Phases of Regulation & Peptic Ulcer*** Management
slides.p: Gastric acid secretion is regulated in three phases, and imbalance between aggressive and protective factors causes peptic ulcer***:
bullets: Three Phases: 1. Cephalic Phase (~30%): Sight/smell/taste/chewing → vagus (blocked by vagotomy). 2. Gastric Phase (~60%): Distension (vagovagal reflex) + peptides/amino acids (stimulate G-cells → Gastrin). 3. Intestinal Phase (~10%): Early duodenal distension stimulates; acid/fat in duodenum triggers enterogastric reflex & enterogastrones (Secretin, CCK, GIP) to inhibit acid.

Peptic Ulcer*** Etiology: Imbalance between aggressive factors (HCl, pepsin, Helicobacter pylori infection, NSAIDs blocking protective prostaglandins, smoking) and mucosal barrier (mucus-bicarbonate layer, tight junctions, mucosal blood flow).

Physiological Basis of Treatment: 1. Proton Pump Inhibitors (Omeprazole) — irreversibly block H⁺–K⁺ ATPase; 2. H₂-Receptor Blockers (Ranitidine/Famotidine) — block histamine potentiation; 3. Antacids & Sucralfate / Misoprostol (PGE₁ analog); 4. Triple therapy antibiotics for H. pylori; 5. Highly selective vagotomy.
slides.remember: Cephalic (30%) + Gastric (60%) + Intestinal (10%)! Ulcer treatment = PPIs (H⁺–K⁺ ATPase) + H₂ blockers + H. pylori eradication!
slides.q: Which phase accounts for the largest proportion (~60%) of daily gastric acid secretion?
slides.why: The gastric phase—driven by stomach distension and protein digestion products stimulating gastrin release—accounts for ~60% of gastric secretion.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Gastric glands & cell types → Gastric juice composition → Mechanism of HCl secretion (with parietal cell diagram) → Three phases of regulation → Peptic ulcer*** (mucosal barrier vs aggressive factors, H. pylori/NSAIDs, physiological basis of drugs & surgery).

lessons.title: Regulation of Gastric Motility & Gastric Emptying*

slides.h: 1. Gastric Motility Patterns & Factors Regulating Gastric Emptying*
slides.p: The stomach stores food via receptive relaxation (vagally mediated), mixes it into chyme via peristaltic waves (3/min) driven by interstitial cells of Cajal, and empties it steadily through the pyloric pump:
bullets: Factors Promoting Gastric Emptying (Gastric Factors): 1. Gastric volume / distension (activates myenteric & vagovagal reflexes) and 2. Gastrin hormone (enhances pyloric pump activity). Liquids empty fastest (~1–2 h), followed by carbohydrates, proteins, and fats (slowest, 4–6 h).

Factors Inhibiting Gastric Emptying (Duodenal Enterogastric Reflex & Enterogastrones): Presence of 1. Fats (strongest inhibitor — releases CCK & GIP), 2. Acidic chyme (pH <3.5–4) (releases Secretin & triggers neural enterogastric reflex), 3. Hypertonic / hypotonic chyme (duodenal osmoreceptors), and 4. Duodenal distension / protein breakdown products.
slides.remember: Emptying order: Liquids > Carbs > Proteins > Fats! Fats in duodenum = Strongest brake via CCK & Enterogastric reflex!
slides.q: Which nutrient component in the duodenum is the most potent physiological inhibitor of gastric emptying?
slides.why: Fats entering the duodenum strongly stimulate CCK release and the enterogastric inhibitory reflex, slowing gastric emptying to allow adequate time for lipid digestion.

lessons.exam: SN order: Types of gastric motility (receptive relaxation, peristalsis, hunger contractions) → Gastric factors promoting emptying (volume, gastrin, food consistency) → Duodenal factors inhibiting emptying (enterogastric reflex + enterogastrones: CCK, secretin, GIP).

lessons.title: Pancreatic Juice & GIT Hormones (Gastrin, CCK, Secretin)

slides.h: 1. Composition, Functions & Regulation of Pancreatic Juice
slides.p: Exocrine pancreas secretes 1.2–1.5 L/day of alkaline pancreatic juice (pH 8.0–8.3) consisting of two distinct components:
bullets: 1. Aqueous HCO₃⁻-Rich Component (from Centroacinar & Ductal Cells — stimulated by SECRETIN): Neutralizes acidic gastric chyme in duodenum (protecting mucosa & providing optimal alkaline pH for pancreatic enzymes).

2. Enzyme-Rich Component (from Acinar Cells — stimulated by CCK & Vagus): Proteolytic (Trypsinogen [activated by brush-border enterokinase → trypsin, which activates all others!], Chymotrypsinogen, Procarboxypeptidase, Proelastase — protected inside acini by trypsin inhibitor!), Amylolytic (Pancreatic α-amylase), and Lipolytic (Pancreatic lipase, colipase, cholesterol esterase, phospholipase A₂).
Phases of Regulation: Cephalic (20%, vagal), Gastric (5–10%, gastrin/vagovagal), and Intestinal Phase (70–80%) via Secretin (acid → watery HCO₃⁻) and CCK (fat/peptides → enzyme-rich).
slides.remember: Secretin = Watery HCO₃⁻ (from duct cells in response to Acid). CCK = Enzyme-rich juice (from acinar cells in response to Fat/Protein)!
slides.q: Which brush-border enzyme in the duodenal mucosa converts inactive trypsinogen into active trypsin?
slides.why: Enterokinase on the duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen to active trypsin, which then autocatalytically activates the remaining pancreatic zymogens.

slides.h: 2. Major Gastrointestinal Hormones (Gastrin, CCK, Secretin, GIP, Motilin)
slides.p: Summarize the site of secretion, stimulus, and actions of key GIT hormones:
bullets: Gastrin (G-cells of gastric antrum): Stimulated by peptides/amino acids, gastric distension, vagal GRP; inhibited by antral pH <2 & somatostatin. Actions: ↑HCl & pepsinogen secretion, ↑gastric motility, trophic to gastric mucosa.

Cholecystokinin / CCK (I-cells of duodenum/jejunum): Stimulated by fatty acids & peptides. Actions: Contracts gallbladder, relaxes sphincter of Oddi, stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic juice, and inhibits gastric emptying.
Secretin (S-cells of duodenum — first hormone discovered!): Stimulated by duodenal acid (pH <4.5). Actions: Stimulates HCO₃⁻-rich pancreatic & biliary secretion, inhibits gastric acid & motility.
GIP (K-cells) & Motilin (M-cells): GIP stimulates insulin release (incretin effect); Motilin initiates interdigestive Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) every 90 min.
slides.remember: Gastrin (G-cells) = Acid & motility. CCK (I-cells) = Gallbladder contraction + Pancreatic enzymes. Secretin (S-cells) = HCO₃⁻!
slides.q: Which gastrointestinal hormone causes gallbladder contraction, relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, and secretion of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice?
slides.why: CCK secreted by duodenal I-cells in response to dietary fat and peptides coordinates gallbladder contraction, sphincter of Oddi relaxation, and pancreatic enzyme release.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Pancreatic juice (volume, pH, composition table, enterokinase activation & trypsin inhibitor, Cephalic/Gastric/Intestinal regulation via Secretin & CCK, steatorrhea in deficiency) → GIT hormones table (Gastrin, CCK, Secretin, GIP, Motilin).
lessons.subject: Physiology

lessons.title: Functions of Bile Salts** & Absorption of Fat

slides.h: 1. Composition of Bile & Six Functions of Bile Salts**
slides.p: Hepatocytes secrete 500–1000 mL/day of bile (concentrated ~10-fold in gallbladder), containing water, electrolytes, bile salts (sodium & potassium glycocholate and taurocholate — derived from cholesterol), bile pigments (bilirubin), phospholipids (lecithin), and cholesterol:
bullets: 1. Emulsification of Fats: Detergent action lowers surface tension, breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets (<1 µm) to increase surface area for pancreatic lipase.

2. Micelle Formation (Hydrotropic Action): Amphipathic bile salts form water-soluble mixed micelles (3–6 nm) carrying monoglycerides, free fatty acids, cholesterol, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) across the unstirred water layer to enterocyte brush border.
3. Activation of Lipases: Activates bile-salt-stimulated lipase and works with colipase.
4. Choleretic Action: Reabsorbed bile salts stimulate hepatocytes to secrete more bile.
5. Keeps Cholesterol in Solution: Prevents cholesterol gallstone precipitation (aided by lecithin).
6. Enterohepatic Circulation: ~95% of bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum via portal vein back to liver (recirculates 6–8 times/day!).
slides.remember: Bile salts = Emulsification + Micelle formation (A, D, E, K absorption) + Choleretic + Keeps cholesterol soluble + Reabsorbed in Terminal Ileum!
slides.q: Where in the gastrointestinal tract are ~95% of conjugated bile salts actively reabsorbed into the enterohepatic circulation?
slides.why: Apical Na⁺-dependent bile acid transporters in the terminal ileum actively reabsorb ~95% of bile salts for return to the liver via the portal vein.

slides.h: 2. Digestion & Absorption of Fat (Chylomicron Pathway)
slides.p: Trace dietary triglycerides from the intestinal lumen into the lacteals:
bullets: 1. Luminal Hydrolysis & Micelles: Emulsified triglycerides are hydrolyzed by pancreatic lipase + colipase into 2-monoglycerides + 2 free fatty acids, packaged into bile salt micelles.

2. Enterocyte Uptake & Re-esterification: Lipids diffuse across apical membrane (bile salts stay behind in lumen); inside smooth ER, long-chain fatty acids (>10–12 C) & monoglycerides are re-esterified into triglycerides.

3. Chylomicron Exocytosis into Lacteals: Triglycerides + cholesterol esters + phospholipids + ApoB-48 form chylomicrons, which exit basolaterally by exocytosis into central lymphatic lacteals → thoracic duct! (Short/medium-chain fatty acids <10 C pass directly into portal blood!).
slides.remember: Long-chain fats → Re-esterified in enterocyte → Chylomicrons (ApoB-48) → Lymphatic Lacteals → Thoracic Duct!
slides.q: In which lipoprotein form are long-chain triglycerides exported from intestinal enterocytes into lymphatic lacteals?
slides.why: Long-chain fatty acids are re-esterified into triglycerides inside enterocytes, packaged with ApoB-48 into chylomicrons, and secreted into intestinal lacteals.

lessons.exam: SN order: Bile composition (liver vs gallbladder bile) → Six functions of bile salts** & enterohepatic circulation → Steps of fat absorption (emulsification, pancreatic lipase, micelles, re-esterification, chylomicron exocytosis into lacteals, steatorrhea note).
lessons.subject: Physiology

lessons.title: Movements of Small & Large Intestine, Peristaltic Rush & Defecation Reflex*

slides.h: 1. Small Intestine Movements & Peristaltic Rush
slides.p: Small intestinal motility mixes chyme with digestive secretions and propels it aborally:
bullets: 1. Segmentation Contractions (Mixing): Ring-like contractions of circular smooth muscle dividing chyme into segments and re-dividing it (paced by BER: 12/min in duodenum, 8/min in ileum) — maximizes mucosal contact for absorption.
2. Peristalsis (Propulsive — Law of Gut): Orad contraction (ACh, Substance P) + caudad receptive relaxation (VIP, NO) mediated by myenteric plexus.
3. Peristaltic Rush: Intense, rapid peristaltic waves sweeping the entire small intestine within minutes to flush out irritants, toxins, or infectious agents (seen in acute infectious diarrhea).
4. Migrating Motor Complex (MMC): Interdigestive housekeeping waves every ~90 min (driven by motilin).
slides.remember: Segmentation = Mixing. Peristalsis = Propulsion. Peristaltic rush = Rapid flushing of irritants! MMC = Fasting housekeeping (Motilin)!
slides.q: Which gastrointestinal hormone initiates the interdigestive Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) during fasting?
slides.why: Motilin released during fasting initiates cyclical Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) waves that clear residual debris from the stomach and small intestine.

slides.h: 2. Large Intestine Movements & Defecation Reflex*
slides.p: The colon absorbs water/electrolytes and stores feces until coordinated elimination:
bullets: Colon Movements: Haustrations (sacculated mixing contractions) and Mass Movements (1–3 times/day, especially after breakfast via gastrocolic reflex, propelling feces into rectum).

Defecation Reflex*: Rectal distension (~25% capacity) activates: 1. Intrinsic myenteric reflex (weak peristalsis in descending/sigmoid colon & rectum + relaxation of internal anal sphincter) reinforced by 2. Parasympathetic spinal defecation reflex (S2, S3, S4 — pelvic splanchnic nerves) (strong colonic contraction + internal sphincter relaxation). Voluntary relaxation of external anal sphincter (pudendal nerve, S2–S4) + Valsalva maneuver completes defecation.
slides.remember: Mass movements = Gastrocolic reflex after meals! Spinal defecation center = S2, S3, S4 (Pelvic splanchnic nerves)!
slides.q: Which spinal cord segments house the parasympathetic defecation center innervating the distal colon, rectum, and internal anal sphincter?
slides.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves arising from sacral segments S2, S3, and S4 mediate the parasympathetic spinal defecation reflex.

lessons.exam: SN order: Small intestine movements (segmentation, peristalsis, peristaltic rush, MMC) → Large intestine movements (haustrations, mass movements/gastrocolic reflex) → Defecation reflex* (intrinsic myenteric + S2–S4 parasympathetic reflex + voluntary external sphincter control).
lessons.subject: Physiology

lessons.title: Anterior Pituitary, Growth Hormone*, Dwarfism & Diabetes Insipidus*

slides.h: 1. Anterior Pituitary Hormones & Metabolic/Growth Actions of Growth Hormone*
slides.p: The adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) secretes six major tropic/peptide hormones from distinct cell types (acidophils: somatotrophs & lactotrophs; basophils: corticotrophs, thyrotrophs, gonadotrophs): GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, and Prolactin:
bullets: Growth Hormone* (Somatotropin) — Growth & Somatomedins: Stimulates linear bone growth before epiphyseal fusion via hepatic/local Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1 / somatomedin C) acting on chondrocytes.

Metabolic Actions of GH*: 1. Protein: Anabolic — increases amino acid transport into cells, stimulates ribosomal protein synthesis, decreases protein catabolism (positive nitrogen balance). 2. Fat: Lipolytic — mobilizes free fatty acids from adipose tissue for energy. 3. Carbohydrate: Diabetogenic / anti-insulin — decreases peripheral glucose uptake and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis (raising blood glucose).
Insulin's Role in Growth: Permissive/anabolic — required alongside GH for protein synthesis and normal somatic growth.
slides.remember: GH = Protein anabolic + Fat lipolytic + Blood glucose UP (anti-insulin/diabetogenic) via IGF-1!
slides.q: What is the primary metabolic effect of Growth Hormone on adipose tissue and blood glucose?
opts: Stimulates lipogenesis and lowers blood glucose
Promotes lipolysis (free fatty acid release) and raises blood glucose (anti-insulin effect)
Inhibits protein synthesis and lowers blood glucose
Stimulates glycogen synthesis in skeletal muscle only
slides.why: Growth hormone mobilizes fat stores (lipolysis) and antagonizes insulin action in peripheral tissues while promoting gluconeogenesis, tending to elevate blood glucose.

slides.h: 2. Dwarfism (Pituitary vs Thyroid) & Diabetes Insipidus vs Diabetes Mellitus*
slides.p: Compare these classic endocrine clinical pairs clearly for LAQs and Short Notes:
bullets: Pituitary Dwarfism vs Thyroid Dwarfism (Cretinism): Pituitary dwarfism (GH deficiency) has proportionate body build, normal intelligence, and delayed bone age. Thyroid dwarfism / cretinism (congenital T₃/T₄ deficiency) has disproportionate build (short limbs relative to trunk, large head), severe mental retardation, coarse features, macroglossia, and umbilical hernia.

Diabetes Insipidus vs Diabetes Mellitus*: Diabetes insipidus = ADH (vasopressin) deficiency/resistance → huge volume of dilute, low-specific-gravity urine (polyuria + polydipsia) with NO glycosuria and normal blood glucose. Diabetes mellitus = insulin deficiency/resistance → hyperglycemia + glycosuria + osmotic diuresis.
slides.remember: Pituitary dwarf = Proportionate + Smart! Thyroid dwarf (Cretin) = Disproportionate + Mentally retarded! Diabetes insipidus = Dilute urine, NO sugar in urine!
slides.q: Which feature distinguishes pituitary dwarfism from congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism)?
opts: Proportionate body proportions and normal intelligence
slides.why: Pituitary dwarfs have proportionate limb-to-trunk growth and normal intelligence, whereas cretins have disproportionate growth and intellectual impairment.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Anterior pituitary hormones → GH* growth (IGF-1) & metabolic actions (protein, lipid, carbohydrate) → Pituitary vs Thyroid dwarfism table → Diabetes insipidus vs Diabetes mellitus* comparison.
lessons.subject: Physiology

lessons.title: Thyroid Hormone Synthesis*, Mechanism, Goitre, Hypothyroidism & Antithyroid Drugs

slides.h: 1. Seven Steps of Thyroid Hormone Synthesis & Release (Diagram)
slides.p: Follicular cells of the thyroid synthesize thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃ — 3–4× more potent and faster-acting) on thyroglobulin in seven steps:
bullets: 1. Iodide Trapping: Active secondary transport via basolateral Na⁺/I⁻ symporter (NIS) (stimulated by TSH; inhibited by thiocyanate/perchlorate).
2. Oxidation of Iodide: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidizes I⁻ to reactive iodine/hypoiodous species using H₂O₂.
3. Organification (Iodination of Tyrosine): TPO attaches iodine to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin → MIT (monoiodotyrosine) and DIT (diiodotyrosine).
4. Coupling: TPO couples DIT + DIT → T₄ and MIT + DIT → T₃ (stored in colloid).

5. Endocytosis & Proteolysis: TSH stimulates colloid endocytosis; lysosomal proteases cleave T₃ and T₄ from thyroglobulin (unneeded MIT & DIT are deiodinated by iodotyrosine deiodinase to recycle iodide).
6–7. Secretion & Peripheral Conversion: T₃/T₄ enter blood (bound mostly to Thyroxine-Binding Globulin / TBG); peripheral deiodinases convert T₄ → T₃.
slides.remember: NIS traps I⁻ → TPO oxidizes, organifies (MIT/DIT) & couples (DIT+DIT = T₄; MIT+DIT = T₃) → TSH triggers release!
slides.q: Which enzyme catalyzes oxidation of iodide, iodination of tyrosine residues, and coupling of iodotyrosines in the thyroid gland?
slides.why: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) mediates iodide oxidation, organification (forming MIT and DIT), and coupling to form T₃ and T₄.

slides.h: 2. Mechanism of Action, Hypothyroidism, Goitre & Antithyroid Drugs
slides.p: Lipophilic T₃/T₄ enter target cells and bind intranuclear thyroid hormone receptors (TR) to regulate gene transcription (↑Na⁺–K⁺ ATPase, ↑BMR, ↑calorigenesis, ↑β-adrenergic sensitivity, CNS/skeletal maturation):
bullets: Hypothyroidism (Myxedema in Adults): Low BMR, cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia, constipation, dry coarse skin, periorbital puffiness, delayed relaxation of ankle jerk, and elevated serum TSH (in primary hypothyroidism).
Endemic Goitre: Dietary iodine deficiency lowers T₃/T₄ → removes negative feedback → chronic TSH hypersecretion causes thyroid follicular hyperplasia and enlargement.
Antithyroid Drugs: Propylthiouracil (PTU) and Methimazole/Carbimazole inhibit TPO (blocking organification & coupling); PTU also inhibits peripheral T₄ → T₃ conversion.
slides.remember: Low iodine → Low T₃/T₄ → High TSH → Goitre! PTU & Carbimazole inhibit TPO; PTU also blocks T₄ → T₃ conversion!
slides.q: Why does dietary iodine deficiency lead to enlargement of the thyroid gland (endemic goitre)?
opts: Direct stimulation of thyroid growth by iodine
Reduced thyroid hormone negative feedback causing increased pituitary TSH secretion
slides.why: Insufficient iodine impairs T₃ and T₄ synthesis; lowered circulating thyroid hormones stimulate excess TSH release, driving follicular hypertrophy and goitre.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Thyroid anatomy/follicles → 7 steps of T₃/T₄ synthesis & release (labelled diagram) → Nuclear receptor mechanism & physiological actions → Hypothyroidism & endemic goitre → Action of antithyroid drugs (PTU/methimazole).

lessons.title: Adrenal Cortex, Glucocorticoids, Aldosterone Regulation & Cushing Syndrome*

slides.h: 1. Adrenal Cortex Zones, Glucocorticoid Actions & Deficiency
slides.p: The adrenal cortex has three zones: Zona glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids — aldosterone), Zona fasciculata (glucocorticoids — cortisol), and Zona reticularis (adrenal androgens — DHEA):
bullets: Regulation of Cortisol: Hypothalamic CRH → anterior pituitary ACTH → cortisol (circadian peak early morning ~6–8 AM; negative feedback on CRH & ACTH).

Cortisol Actions (Intracellular/Nuclear Receptor): 1. Metabolic: ↑Hepatic gluconeogenesis & glycogen deposition, ↓peripheral glucose uptake (anti-insulin), ↑protein breakdown in muscle/lymphoid/bone, ↑lipolysis/fat redistribution. 2. Anti-inflammatory & Immunosuppressive: Induces lipocortin-1 (annexin A1) inhibiting phospholipase A₂ (↓prostaglandins & leukotrienes), stabilizes lysosomes, inhibits histamine/cytokines. 3. Permissive & Vascular: Maintains vascular responsiveness to catecholamines & GFR.
Deficiency (Addison's Disease): Hypotension, hypoglycemia, weakness, hyperpigmentation (high ACTH acting on MC₁ receptors).
slides.remember: Cortisol = Stress hormone + Gluconeogenesis + Lipocortin-1 (anti-inflammatory) + Permissive for catecholamines!
slides.q: Which protein induced by glucocorticoids inhibits phospholipase A₂ to exert anti-inflammatory effects?
slides.why: Glucocorticoids induce synthesis of lipocortin-1 (annexin A1), which inhibits phospholipase A₂ and decreases prostaglandin and leukotriene formation.

slides.h: 2. Factors Regulating Aldosterone & Cushing Syndrome* Features
slides.p: Contrast how aldosterone is regulated vs cortisol, and recognize Cushing syndrome:
bullets: Four Factors Regulating Aldosterone Secretion: 1. Angiotensin II (via RAAS — major stimulus), 2. Elevated extracellular K⁺ (hyperkalemia) (direct depolarizing stimulus on zona glomerulosa), 3. ACTH (modest acute permissive/stimulatory effect), and 4. ANP (Atrial Natriuretic Peptide) (inhibits aldosterone).

Cushing Syndrome* (Chronic Excess Glucocorticoids): Moon face, buffalo hump, central truncal obesity with thin wasted limbs, purplish abdominal striae, hyperglycemia/steroid diabetes, hypertension, muscle weakness, and osteoporosis.
slides.remember: Aldosterone stimulators = Angiotensin II + High K⁺ + ACTH; Inhibitor = ANP! Cushing = Moon face + Buffalo hump + Central obesity + Hyperglycemia!
slides.q: Which of the following is a direct stimulator of aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa?
slides.why: Elevated extracellular K⁺ directly depolarizes zona glomerulosa cells and stimulates aldosterone synthesis/secretion to promote K⁺ excretion.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Cortical zones & hormones → Glucocorticoid regulation (CRH–ACTH) & actions → Deficiency → Factors regulating aldosterone → Cushing syndrome* clinical features.

lessons.title: Calcium Regulation*, Parathyroid Hormone, Tetany & Insulin

slides.h: 1. Calcium Homeostasis, PTH, Calcitriol, Calcitonin & Tetany
slides.p: Normal total plasma calcium is 9–11 mg/dL (~2.2–2.7 mmol/L), with ionized Ca²⁺ (~50%) being the physiologically active fraction essential for neuromuscular excitability, muscle contraction, coagulation, and second-messenger signaling:
bullets: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH — 84 aa, CaSR-regulated): Raises plasma Ca²⁺ and lowers plasma PO₄³⁻ by: (a) Bone: Stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption (via RANKL on osteoblasts); (b) Kidney: Increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT, decreases PO₄³⁻ reabsorption in PCT (phosphaturic), and stimulates 1α-hydroxylase to form active Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)₂D₃); (c) Gut (indirect via Calcitriol): Increases intestinal Ca²⁺ & PO₄³⁻ absorption.
Calcitonin (Parafollicular C-cells): Lowers plasma Ca²⁺ (inhibits osteoclasts; minor role in adult humans).

Hypocalcemic Tetany (Signs & Treatment): Low ionized Ca²⁺ increases neuronal Na⁺ channel excitability → neuromuscular hyperexcitability: carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, Chvostek's sign (facial twitch on tapping facial nerve), and Trousseau's sign (carpal spasm on inflating BP cuff above systolic BP for 3 min). Treated with IV calcium gluconate + vitamin D/PTH correction.
slides.remember: PTH = ↑Plasma Ca²⁺, ↓Plasma PO₄³⁻, ↑1,25-(OH)₂D₃! Tetany = Low Ca²⁺ → Chvostek's & Trousseau's signs → Treat with IV Calcium!
slides.q: Spasm of the hand/wrist (carpopedal spasm) induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for up to 3 minutes is known as:
slides.why: Trousseau's sign is a classic clinical sign of latent hypocalcemic tetany elicited by cuff-induced ischemia/compression.

slides.h: 2. Functions & Secretion of Insulin
slides.p: Insulin (β-cells of islets of Langerhans) is the principal anabolic hormone lowering blood glucose:
bullets: Secretion Stimuli: Glucose (enters β-cell via GLUT2 → glucokinase → ↑ATP/ADP ratio → closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels → depolarization → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin exocytosis!), amino acids, vagal ACh, GIP/GLP-1.

Key Functions: 1. Glucose: Inserts GLUT4 in skeletal muscle & adipose tissue to lower blood glucose; stimulates glycogenesis & inhibits gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis; 2. Lipid: Stimulates lipogenesis & inhibits lipolysis; 3. Protein: Stimulates amino acid uptake & protein synthesis (anabolic growth).
slides.remember: β-cell glucose sensing: ↑Glucose → ↑ATP → Closes K_ATP channel → Depolarization → Ca²⁺ influx → Insulin release! GLUT4 = Insulin-dependent!
slides.q: In pancreatic β-cells, how does an increase in extracellular glucose trigger insulin secretion?
opts: Opening ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels to hyperpolarize the membrane
Increasing intracellular ATP/ADP ratio, closing K_ATP channels, depolarizing the membrane, and opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
slides.why: Glucose metabolism elevates ATP, closing ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels, depolarizing the β-cell membrane, and triggering Ca²⁺-dependent insulin exocytosis.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Plasma Ca²⁺ levels & roles → PTH & Calcitriol regulation of Ca²⁺/PO₄³⁻ → Tetany (Chvostek's, Trousseau's, treatment) & Osteoporosis → Insulin secretion & metabolic functions.

lessons.title: Menstrual Cycle, Ovulation, Contraception***, Spermatogenesis*, Pregnancy & Parturition

slides.h: 1. Menstrual Cycle, Ovulation & Contraception***
slides.p: A typical 28-day menstrual cycle coordinates ovarian and endometrial events under hypothalamic GnRH and pituitary FSH/LH control:
bullets: Ovarian & Endometrial Phases: 1. Menstrual phase (Days 1–5): Shedding of functional endometrium as estrogen & progesterone fall. 2. Follicular / Proliferative phase (Days 6–14): FSH matures Graafian follicle; rising estrogen repairs/proliferates endometrium (and exerts positive feedback on LH just before ovulation). 3. Ovulation (Day 14 in 28-day cycle): Triggered by LH surge (~24–36 h before ovum release). 4. Luteal / Secretory phase (Days 15–28): Corpus luteum secretes progesterone + estrogen → secretory glands & spiral arteries develop; if no fertilization, corpus luteum regresses into corpus albicans.
Indicators of Ovulation: Mid-cycle LH surge, rise in basal body temperature (BBT ~0.3–0.5°C due to progesterone), thin watery ferning cervical mucus, and secretory endometrium.
Contraception***: Combined oral contraceptive pills (estrogen + progestin) suppress GnRH/FSH/LH to inhibit ovulation, thicken cervical mucus, and alter endometrium; barrier/IUCD/rhythm methods.
slides.remember: LH surge triggers Ovulation (Day 14)! Progesterone dominates Luteal phase & raises Basal Body Temperature! OCPs inhibit ovulation!
slides.q: Which hormonal event directly precedes and triggers ovulation around Day 14 of a 28-day menstrual cycle?
opts: Sharp drop in both estrogen and progesterone
slides.why: Sustained high estrogen prior to mid-cycle triggers a surge of LH (and a smaller FSH surge), inducing ovulation.

slides.h: 2. Spermatogenesis*, Pregnancy Changes, Circulatory Changes at Birth & Parturition
slides.p: Cover the remaining Reproductive System short-note essentials cleanly:
bullets: Spermatogenesis* (~64–74 days in seminiferous tubules): Spermatogonia (2n) → Primary spermatocytes (2n) → Meiosis I → Secondary spermatocytes (n) → Meiosis II → Spermatids (n) → Spermiogenesis (maturation into spermatozoa supported by Sertoli cells; requires ~32–34°C scrotal temperature, FSH, and intratesticular testosterone).
Pregnancy & Last Trimester: ↑Blood volume (+30–40%), ↑CO (+30–50%), ↑GFR (+40–50%), ↑ventilation, lordosis, breast enlargement, hCG/estrogen/progesterone.

Circulatory Changes at Birth: First breath expands lungs → ↓pulmonary vascular resistance & ↑systemic resistance → foramen ovale closes (flap pushed against septum secundum), ductus arteriosus constricts (↑PO₂ & ↓prostaglandins → ligamentum arteriosum), and ductus venosus closes (ligamentum venosum).

Parturition (Ferguson Reflex): Fetal head stretches cervix → afferent signals to hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases Oxytocin → uterine contractions + cervical stretch (positive feedback loop) until delivery.
slides.remember: Birth: First breath → Foramen ovale & Ductus arteriosus close! Ferguson reflex = Cervical stretch → Oxytocin → Uterine contractions!
slides.q: Which circulatory change occurs shortly after birth when pulmonary vascular resistance drops and left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure?
opts: Functional closure of the foramen ovale
Reversal of flow through the umbilical arteries
slides.why: Lung inflation lowers pulmonary resistance and increases pulmonary venous return to the left atrium, pressing the septum primum against the septum secundum to close the foramen ovale.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Menstrual cycle phases & hormones (diagram) → Ovulation indicators & contraception*** → Spermatogenesis* → Pregnancy/last trimester & birth circulatory changes → Parturition & oxytocin.

lessons.title: Pulmonary Ventilation, Work of Breathing*, Lung Compliance*, Surfactant* & FRC

slides.h: 1. Mechanism of Breathing, Work of Breathing* & Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)
slides.p: During quiet inspiration, contraction of the diaphragm (descends ~1.5 cm, accounting for ~75% of resting tidal volume) and external intercostals expands thoracic volume, making alveolar (intrapulmonary) pressure slightly subatmospheric (−1 cmH₂O) so air flows inward; quiet expiration is passive via elastic recoil:
bullets: Work of Breathing* (~3–5% of resting energy expenditure): Three components — 1. Compliance work (stretching elastic lungs & chest wall), 2. Tissue resistance work (viscous drag of lung tissue), and 3. Airway resistance work (airflow friction through bronchi; rises sharply in asthma/bronchoconstriction).

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC ≈ 2.2–2.4 L = ERV + RV): Volume of air remaining in lungs at end of normal quiet expiration; acts as a 'buffer reservoir' that smooths arterial PO₂/PCO₂ between breaths and keeps small airways/alveoli open.
slides.remember: FRC = ERV + RV (~2.3 L) = Air buffer smoothing blood gases between breaths! Work of breathing = Elastic + Tissue + Airway resistance work!
slides.q: What is the primary physiological role of Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) in the lungs?
opts: To act as an air reservoir buffering blood gas (O₂/CO₂) levels continuously between breaths
To force residual air out during quiet expiration
slides.why: FRC maintains a steady volume of alveolar gas throughout the respiratory cycle, preventing wide swings in alveolar PO₂ and PCO₂ between breaths.

slides.h: 2. Lung Compliance*, Surfactant* & Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
slides.p: Lung compliance (C = ΔV / ΔP ≈ 200 mL/cmH₂O) measures distensibility of the lungs and is governed heavily by alveolar surface tension:
bullets: Pulmonary Surfactant* (Synthesized by Type II Alveolar Pneumocytes from ~24–28 weeks gestation): Composed mainly of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) phospholipid + surfactant proteins (SP-A, B, C, D). Lowers alveolar surface tension (Law of Laplace: P = 2T / r), prevents collapse of small alveoli into large ones, increases compliance, and keeps alveoli dry.

Neonatal RDS / Hyaline Membrane Disease: Surfactant deficiency in premature infants causes high surface tension, alveolar collapse (atelectasis), low compliance, stiff lungs, and severe hypoxemia/work of breathing.
slides.remember: Type II pneumocytes make Surfactant (DPPC) → lowers surface tension (Law of Laplace: P = 2T/r) → prevents alveolar collapse!
slides.q: According to Laplace's law (P = 2T / r), how does pulmonary surfactant prevent collapse of smaller alveoli?
opts: By increasing surface tension (T) selectively in small alveoli
By lowering surface tension (T) more strongly in smaller alveoli where surfactant molecules are more concentrated
By increasing alveolar radius (r) during expiration
By increasing intrapleural pressure above atmospheric pressure
slides.why: Because surfactant molecules pack closer together when a small alveolus deflates, surface tension (T) drops further, stabilizing smaller alveoli against collapse.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Mechanism of inspiration & expiration → Work of breathing* (3 components) → FRC (ERV + RV, physiological role) → Lung compliance* & Surfactant* (Type II cells, DPPC, Laplace law, RDS/hyaline membrane disease).

lessons.title: Respiratory Membrane*, O₂–Hb Dissociation Curve**, Bohr & Haldane Effects

slides.h: 1. Respiratory Membrane*, O₂ Transport & O₂–Hb Dissociation Curve**
slides.p: Gaseous exchange occurs across the ultra-thin respiratory membrane (~0.2–0.6 µm thick) via passive diffusion (Fick's law of diffusion: proportional to surface area & partial pressure gradient, inversely proportional to thickness):
bullets: O₂ Transport: ~98.5% bound to hemoglobin (oxyhemoglobin) (~20 mL O₂/100 mL blood at PO₂ ~100 mmHg) and ~1.5% dissolved in plasma.
Sigmoidal O₂–Hb Curve** & P₅₀: Sigmoidal shape reflects cooperative binding of 4 O₂ molecules to heme. P₅₀ is the PO₂ at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (~26–27 mmHg).
Right Shift (Decreased O₂ Affinity — Unloads O₂ to Tissues): Caused by ↑CO₂ / ↓pH (Bohr effect), ↑Temperature, and ↑2,3-BPG (2,3-DPG) (e.g., high altitude, anemia, exercising muscle).
slides.remember: Bohr effect = High CO₂ / Low pH (active tissues) shifts O₂–Hb curve to RIGHT to unload O₂! Normal P₅₀ ≈ 27 mmHg!
slides.q: Which change in active exercising skeletal muscle shifts the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT and facilitates O₂ unloading?
opts: Increased PCO₂, decreased pH (Bohr effect), increased temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG
slides.why: Higher PCO₂, lower pH (lactic acid/CO₂), higher temperature, and elevated 2,3-BPG reduce hemoglobin's O₂ affinity (right shift), releasing more O₂ to working tissues.

slides.h: 2. CO₂ Transport, Haldane Effect & Pulmonary Circulation
slides.p: CO₂ is transported in blood in three forms: ~70% as Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) (via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs + chloride shift / Hamburger phenomenon), ~20–25% as carbamino compounds (carbaminohemoglobin), and ~5–10% dissolved:
bullets: Haldane Effect: Deoxygenation of hemoglobin increases its ability to carry CO₂ (and buffer H⁺) in systemic tissues, whereas oxygenation of Hb in the lungs promotes CO₂ release! (Deoxyhemoglobin is a weaker acid than oxyhemoglobin).

Pulmonary Circulation: Low-pressure (~25/8 mmHg, mean ~15 mmHg), low-resistance circuit; hypoxia causes VASOCONSTRICTION in pulmonary arterioles (diverting blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli to better-ventilated ones — opposite of systemic vessels!).
slides.remember: Bohr = O₂ unloading aided by CO₂/H⁺. Haldane = CO₂ unloading in lungs aided by O₂ binding to Hb! Hypoxia CONSTRICTS pulmonary vessels!
slides.q: How does oxygenation of hemoglobin in the pulmonary capillaries affect carbon dioxide transport (the Haldane effect)?
opts: It increases hemoglobin's affinity for CO₂
It reduces hemoglobin's affinity for CO₂ and H⁺, promoting CO₂ release into the alveoli
It reverses the chloride shift into RBCs
slides.why: Oxyhemoglobin is a stronger acid than deoxyhemoglobin, driving H⁺ off Hb to combine with HCO₃⁻ and releasing CO₂ from the blood into the alveoli.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Respiratory membrane* layers & diffusion → O₂ transport & sigmoidal O₂–Hb curve** (label axes, P₅₀, Bohr effect & right-shift factors) → CO₂ transport (HCO₃⁻ & chloride shift) & Haldane effect → Pulmonary circulation features.

lessons.title: Neural & Chemical Control of Respiration, Hypoxia***, High Altitude & Thermoregulation***

slides.h: 1. Neural & Chemical Control of Breathing & Periodic Breathing
slides.p: Automatic breathing rhythm is generated by the pre-Bötzinger complex / medullary respiratory centers (DRG & VRG), modulated by the pontine pneumotaxic center (limits inspiration / sets rate) and apneustic center:
bullets: Chemical Control: Central chemoreceptors (ventral medulla) respond primarily to ↑H⁺ in CSF generated by ↑PaCO₂ crossing the blood-brain barrier (most powerful day-to-day drive!). Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid & aortic bodies) respond mainly when PaO₂ falls below ~60 mmHg (also to ↑PaCO₂ & ↓pH).

Periodic Breathing & Ondine's Curse: Cheyne-Stokes breathing (waxing-and-waning tidal volume alternating with apnea, seen in heart failure/brain lesions); Ondine's curse (failure of automatic respiratory drive during sleep).
slides.remember: Central chemoreceptors sense ↑CSF H⁺ (from ↑PaCO₂)! Peripheral chemoreceptors kick in strongly when PaO₂ <60 mmHg!
slides.q: What is the primary chemical stimulus detected by central chemoreceptors on the ventral surface of the medulla?
opts: Increased H⁺ concentration in cerebrospinal fluid (driven by elevated PaCO₂)
slides.why: CO₂ diffuses readily across the blood-brain barrier into CSF, forming H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, which stimulates central chemoreceptors.

slides.h: 2. Hypoxia***, High Altitude Acclimatization & Temperature Regulation (Heat Loss*** & Cold**)
slides.p: Master these high-yield environmental/clinical respiratory & thermoregulatory topics:
bullets: Hypoxia*** (4 Types): 1. Hypoxic hypoxia (low PaO₂ — high altitude, hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt), 2. Anemic hypoxia (low Hb or CO poisoning; PaO₂ is normal!), 3. Stagnant/ischemic hypoxia (low blood flow / heart failure / shock), 4. Histotoxic hypoxia (cyanide blocks cytochrome oxidase; cells cannot use O₂).

High Altitude Acclimatization: Hypoxic hyperventilation → ↑RBC count & Hb (via Erythropoietin / HIF-1α), ↑2,3-BPG, ↑capillary density & mitochondria (Acute Mountain Sickness causes headache, nausea, insomnia, pulmonary/cerebral edema).

Thermoregulation (Hypothalamus — Preoptic anterior = heat loss; Posterior = heat conservation/shivering): Heat loss*** occurs via radiation (~60%), conduction, convection, and evaporation of sweat (only mechanism when ambient temp > body temp!). Extreme cold** causes vasoconstriction, shivering, and non-shivering thermogenesis (brown fat); severe hypothermia (<35°C) depresses metabolism & cardiac conduction.
slides.remember: Hypoxia = Hypoxic, Anemic, Stagnant, Histotoxic! Above body temp, ONLY sweating (evaporation) loses heat! Hypothalamus = Body thermostat!
slides.q: In which type of hypoxia is arterial PO₂ (PaO₂) normal while oxygen delivery to tissues is reduced due to a decreased oxygen-carrying capacity of blood?
slides.why: In anemic hypoxia (or carbon monoxide poisoning), alveolar gas exchange and PaO₂ are normal, but reduced functional hemoglobin lowers total arterial O₂ content.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Neural & chemical respiratory control (DRG/VRG/pneumotaxic, central CSF H⁺, peripheral O₂ <60 mmHg) → Hypoxia*** (4 types) & high-altitude acclimatization → Thermoregulation (hypothalamus, heat loss*** methods, cold** & hypothermia).
